source.original_text: For the two normalized restricted-Gaussian fibers with common potential and quadratic centers y and y', the displayed log-density ratio has spatial gradient eta^{-1}(y-y'). Therefore its relative Fisher information under the left probability fiber is the expectation of the constant squared score, namely eta^{-2} times the squared Euclidean distance between the centers. In the cited proof this value is subsequently inserted into log-Sobolev and Talagrand inequalities. The selected ASTIS edge is only the exact Fisher-energy evaluation for the explicit smooth representative; it is not the log-Sobolev inequality, the Talagrand inequality, or the resulting Wasserstein contraction.

blind_reconstruction.text: For every finite index type iota, let E be the real Euclidean space indexed by iota, with its Euclidean norm and measurable structure. For every probability measure mu on E, every real eta with eta != 0, and every pair of centers y,yprime in E, define Z_y = integral_E exp(-norm(z-y)^2/(2*eta)) dmu(z) and Z_yprime = integral_E exp(-norm(z-yprime)^2/(2*eta)) dmu(z). Define R:E->R by R(t) = -norm(t-y)^2/(2*eta)-log(Z_y)-(-norm(t-yprime)^2/(2*eta))+log(Z_yprime). With constant weight q(t)=1, the relative Fisher functional, defined here as information(mu,q,R) = integral_E q(x)*norm(gradient R(x))^2 dmu(x), satisfies the exact equality information(mu,1,R) = (eta^(-1))^2*norm(y-yprime)^2. The gradient is the spatial gradient in the variable t with respect to the Euclidean inner product, and the integration variable in the Fisher functional is x. Both logarithms of integrals are spatial constants. The quantifiers range over all such finite index types, probability measures, nonzero real eta, and centers; the assumptions are only finiteness of the index type, total mass one for mu, and eta != 0. In particular eta need not be positive, mu need not be Gaussian, and no exponential-integrability or strictly-positive-normalizer assumption is stated; all integrals, logarithms, inverses, and powers retain their Lean real-operation meanings. The conclusion is an identity for this explicit function R with unit weight against mu, not an assertion identifying R with a log-likelihood ratio of two measures. The coefficient is exactly eta^(-2), and the right side depends only on eta and the squared distance between the centers, with no explicit dimension factor or dependence on mu beyond its probability normalization.

import AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.InformationTheory.RelativeFisher
import AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.InformationTheory.TiltedLogRatio

/-!
# Relative Fisher energy of quadratic tilt representatives

Lee--Shen--Tian, arXiv:2010.03106v4, Lemma 2, first computes the
relative score between two restricted-Gaussian fibers in equation (11), then
integrates its squared norm under the left fiber.  This file isolates that
second step for the explicit smooth representative.

It does not differentiate Mathlib's canonical measurable `llr`, and it does
not prove a log-Sobolev, Talagrand, or Wasserstein inequality.
-/

namespace AutoSamplingTheory
namespace TechnicalLemmas
namespace InformationTheory
namespace QuadraticTiltFisher

open MeasureTheory
open scoped RealInnerProductSpace

noncomputable section

variable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]

abbrev State := EuclideanSpace ℝ ι

/-- The relative Fisher energy of the explicit normalized quadratic log-ratio
representative is exactly the squared center displacement divided by `eta²`.

The base measure appears only through the two spatially constant normalizers.
The probability assumption is the genuine step that turns the integral of the
constant squared score into that constant.  The paper consumer has `eta > 0`;
the algebraic statement only requires `eta ≠ 0`. -/
theorem information_quadratic_representative
    (mu : Measure (State (ι := ι))) [IsProbabilityMeasure mu]
    {eta : ℝ} (heta : eta ≠ 0) (y y' : State (ι := ι)) :
    RelativeFisher.information mu (fun _ => 1)
        (fun t =>
          -(‖t - y‖ ^ 2 / (2 * eta)) -
            Real.log (∫ z, Real.exp (-(‖z - y‖ ^ 2 / (2 * eta))) ∂mu) -
          (-(‖t - y'‖ ^ 2 / (2 * eta))) +
            Real.log (∫ z, Real.exp (-(‖z - y'‖ ^ 2 / (2 * eta))) ∂mu)) =
      eta⁻¹ ^ 2 * ‖y - y'‖ ^ 2 := by
  rw [RelativeFisher.information]
  simp_rw [RelativeFisher.densityEnergy, one_mul,
    TiltedLogRatio.gradient_quadratic_representative mu heta y y']
  simp [norm_smul, Real.norm_eq_abs, mul_pow]

end

end QuadraticTiltFisher
end InformationTheory
end TechnicalLemmas
end AutoSamplingTheory

lesson.title: The quadratic fiber score has exact relative Fisher energy
lesson.statement: Let μ be any probability measure on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space. For η≠0 and centers y,y′, evaluate relative Fisher information using the explicit normalized quadratic log-ratio representative. Its value is exactly η⁻²‖y−y′‖². The restricted-Gaussian application uses η>0.
assumptions: The integration law μ is a probability measure; this is what turns the integral of a constant into the same constant.
The state space is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and η is nonzero. The paper's fiber variance satisfies η>0.
The argument evaluates the displayed smooth log-ratio representative. It does not differentiate Mathlib's canonical measurable llr representative.

steps.title: Insert the exact score
steps.text: The preceding ASTIS theorem differentiates the displayed quadratic representative genuinely and gives a vector independent of x.

steps.title: Expose the constant integrand
steps.text: Substituting the score in the definition of relative Fisher information leaves a spatially constant squared norm.

steps.title: Use probability mass one
steps.text: Because μ has total mass one, integrating this nonnegative constant does not introduce a mass factor.

steps.title: Pull the scalar out of the norm
steps.text: The norm of a real scalar multiple is its absolute value times the norm. Squaring removes the sign and gives the exact η⁻² coefficient.

lesson.lean_statement: The function supplied to RelativeFisher.information contains both log normalizers explicitly. They are spatial constants and disappear only through the previously proved genuine gradient theorem.
lesson.lean_proof: The proof unfolds the ASTIS relative-Fisher definitions, rewrites every pointwise gradient with the compiled quadratic-score theorem, and lets Mathlib evaluate the constant integral under the probability instance and normalize the scalar norm square.
